summary: Be An Earth System Trend Detective! is a simple web app that helps anyone see how the Earth is changing over time, using real NASA data. The user chooses a variable (for example sea surface temperature, rain, sea ice or plant greenness), a place, and a range of years. The app then answers four easy questions: What is changing? Where is it changing? How much is it changing? Is the change real? It shows a chart with a trend line, a map, and result cards. To check if a change is real, it uses the Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen’s slope, and shows a p-value. It also writes one plain sentence using the real calculated numbers. The app answers the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” by turning large NASA datasets into clear answers for students, teachers and the public. It is important because people should understand real changes on Earth, not guesses.
details:
Be An Earth System Trend Detective! shows how the Earth is changing over many years, using real NASA data. The user picks a variable ([sea surface temperature, rain, sea ice, plants]), a place ([Arabian Sea]), and a range of years ([2000 to 2025]). The app then shows a chart with a trend line, [a map,] and four result cards: What is changing? Where? How much? Is the change real?
How it works

  1. The app reads NASA data stored as CSV files (date, region, value).
  2. It removes the normal yearly (seasonal) pattern, so we can see the real change. This is called an anomaly.
  3. It calculates the trend with Sen’s slope, for example “change every 10 years”.
  4. It checks if the change is real using the Mann-Kendall test and shows the p-value. If p is less than 0.05, the change is marked “significant”.
  5. It writes one simple sentence using only the calculated numbers. It does not make up any findings.

Benefits and impact
The tool makes big NASA datasets easy for students, teachers and the public. It says clearly when a change is not significant. It shows what is changing, not why, unless there is proof. [It works offline, because the data is stored with the project.] Every chart shows units and the NASA data source.
Tools used
[HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website; Plotly for charts; Leaflet for the map; Python (pandas, SciPy) for preparing data.]
What we considered
We tested the trend code with a straight rising line (it must show a very small p-value) and with random data (it must show “not significant”). [We also compared our results with NASA Giovanni.] We kept the design simple so anyone can use it on a phone or a computer.https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1H_H55wWqzG7tv8Wuc7V2bRPN-zV3TTKO?usp=drive_link
